Jeeps may be uncomplex to work on, but Jeep has a poor record since 2000 - 11 of the 16 model years since the turn of the millennium have had more complaints & issues reported than the previous year. 11 times out of 16 (69%, more than 2/3 of the time), the next iteration of the Wrangler was worse than the previous one.

Anecdotally, a family member who worked for years as an automobile insurance agent confirms that his real-life experience matches what that data suggests.

I was looking at the Wrangler as a potential new car a while back (ended up going with the Toyota FJ), and was completely un-sold after I discovered that starting in 2014, on all engines except the largest (3.8L, I think), the plastic oil cooler filter, located directly over the engine's V-block, overheats, cracks, dumps the oil (which catches fire if you've been driving for any period of time), and then bricks your engine 'cause it's been running with no oil. There were over 40 complaints about this specific issue filed with the US' National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, community discussion about it going back years - including dealerships being sold out of the replacement part & back-ordered - and at least 2 model years being released with the faulty design. I don't know if they've fixed this in the 2016 wrangler.

I was no longer able to take Jeep's "Trail Rated" classic off-roader, marketing seriously. It feels like the classic Jeeps that built the brand are kin to the classic Humvees - and what's being sold now are as distanced from that as the H3 Truck was from the H1.

I hope you got a good Wrangler - if you've got a 12-year-old Jeep, that looks to be from before things really started to get bad.

But I couldn't advise anyone to purchase a contemporary Wrangler, and wouldn't myself.

My family has been a Toyota family since before I was born. We currently have a sienna chugging along past 300,000 miles and a 19yr old Camry just past 225,000. It replaced a 1980s Camry. I just recently bought a Toyota FJ cruiser.

There's a reason the classic Toyota Land Cruiser was used and still is used all over Africa, and why the Toyota Hilux pickup is used all over the Middle East. They are solid, affordable, reliable vehicles that will take whatever maintenance (or lack thereof) you provide and keep running for years after they, by all rights, should died.

The new Camrys look kinda cool, though the 1980s are still my favorite.

If reliability is a big concern to you, you'd be hard-pressed to do better than a Toyota. However, given that you are thinking about a new car at 7 years, and not 17, perhaps these vehicles offer more reliability than you really need. No sense paying for things you won't use.

That said, you should be aware of what you have paid in repairs on your current car over the past 12 months, and come up with a "monthly payment" equivalent to use to compare to what you would be paying if you got a new car. This is why the Toyotas remain with my family for so long: even after they're paid off and start racking up repair costs, the per month cost remains far less than a new car payment, for many many years. Part of this is because, as mentioned elsewhere, parts are plentiful and cheap. Example: I bought a 70k-mile-newer and 2-year-newer transmission for my Camry for $300 (the original failed at 225k).

If you do the monthly service cost thing on your existing car, and it turns out that it would be far cheaper than the car payment on any new car that you actually want to drive, then maybe resolve to keep it as your backup / sometimes vehicle and get a Harley, if that's something you want.

If you hate paying for maintenance and you know you're gonna swap your next car out as soon as it is paid off and starts racking up repair cost as well, then maybe you don't care about long-term reliability and could get away with paying less for a vehicle, or paying for fun features or performance instead of long-term reliability.

Before You Buy, Look Here

http://www.carcomplaints.com

Pick a Make and Model (e.g. Toyota Camry, Jeep Wrangler, etc) and you will see complaints filed and issues identified with the vehicle over all of its years. Use it like this:

  1. When considering a specific used car, e.g. 1990 Toyota Camry, is it likely to fail on you, and if so, what is likely to fail?
  2. When considering a Make/Model but no specific year, which years were good ones, and which years should be avoided?
  3. When considering buying new, has overall reliability been getting better or worse? The trend should be fewer complaints every year - ever time a newer year has more complaints than a previous year, that's a red flag.

Examples:

  1. Should you buy a 2007 Toyota Camry? Probably not: http://www.carcomplaints.com/Toyota/Camry/
  2. Which year Honda Civics should you consider? Not 2001 and 2006: http://www.carcomplaints.com/Honda/Civic/
  3. Don't buy a Jeep Grand Cherokee (they clearly haven't figured out how to make 'em yet): http://www.carcomplaints.com/Jeep/Grand_Cherokee/
